title: Individual influences on behavior

How to use this sheet: you do not need any background to read it. Start with Key Terms. Each concept then goes: plain English → analogy → 3 core points → for every formula: what it says, when to use it, what each letter means, an everyday example, a step-by-step MCAT example and the trap → where to practice. Read top to bottom once, then use the formulas as a reference.

Key terms (read first)

TermPlain meaning
Neuron / synapseA nerve cell / the tiny gap where one neuron passes a chemical message to the next.
NeurotransmitterA chemical messenger released by a neuron to signal the next cell.
Receptor / agonist / antagonistA protein a chemical fits into like a key in a lock / a drug that switches the receptor on / a drug that blocks it. D₂ is one type of dopamine receptor.
Reuptake / SSRIThe sending neuron pulling its neurotransmitter back in / selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, an antidepressant that blocks serotonin reuptake so more stays in the synapse.
Brain lobesFrontal (front: planning, self-control), parietal (top: touch, space), temporal (sides: hearing, language comprehension), occipital (back: vision).
Limbic systemDeep structures for emotion and memory: amygdala (fear), hippocampus (new memories), hypothalamus (body drives and hormones).
Cerebellum / brainstemThe "little brain" at the back for balance and coordination / the stalk joining brain and spinal cord.
Corpus callosumThe thick cable of fibers connecting the left and right hemispheres (halves of the brain).
LateralizationThe two brain hemispheres specializing in different functions (language is usually left).
HormoneA chemical messenger carried in the blood from a gland to distant targets.
Pituitary / adrenal / pineal glandMaster gland under the brain / glands on the kidneys (cortex makes cortisol, medulla makes epinephrine) / small gland that makes melatonin.
Gene / DNA / alleleA stretch of DNA (the cell's instruction code) for one product / one version of a gene.
Heritability (h²)The share of trait variation in a population linked to genetic variation (0–1).
Correlation (r)A number from −1 to +1 for how closely two things rise and fall together.
VarianceHow spread out a trait is across a group.
ConcordanceThe probability that if one twin has a trait or disorder, the other does too.
Monozygotic (MZ) / dizygotic (DZ) twinsIdentical twins (~100% shared genes) / fraternal twins (~50% shared genes on average).
EpigeneticsChanges in gene expression (whether a gene is switched on), e.g. by DNA methylation (chemical tags), without changes in DNA sequence.
Gene–environment interactionA gene's effect depends on the environment (and vice versa).
PersonalityA person's relatively stable patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving.
UnconsciousMental activity outside awareness.
Id / ego / superegoFreud's parts of the mind: instinctive drives / realistic manager / internalized morals.
Defense mechanismAn unconscious strategy the ego uses to reduce anxiety by distorting reality.
TraitA stable tendency to behave in a certain way across situations.
Self-efficacyBelief in your ability to succeed at a specific task.
Locus of controlBelief that outcomes are controlled internally (by you) or externally (luck, others).
DSM-5The American Psychiatric Association's manual that defines disorders by symptom criteria (current edition DSM-5-TR, 2022).
Psychosis / hallucination / delusionLosing touch with reality / perceiving something that is not there (hearing voices) / a fixed false belief.
Positive / negative symptomsSymptoms that add something (hallucinations) / that take something away (flat affect = little emotional expression; alogia = little speech; avolition = little drive; anhedonia = no pleasure).
Mania / hypomaniaAn abnormally high, energized mood with poor judgment / a milder, shorter form.
Ego-syntonicFelt as a normal part of oneself, so it causes the person little distress.
MotivationThe forces that start, direct and sustain behavior.
Intrinsic / extrinsic motivationDoing something for its own sake / for an outside reward.
HomeostasisKeeping internal conditions (temperature, glucose) stable around a set point.
ArousalThe body's level of activation and alertness.
AttitudeA learned evaluation of a person, object or idea.
Cognitive dissonanceDiscomfort from holding conflicting beliefs or acting against a belief.

A) CORE CONCEPTS

Concept 1: Biological bases of behavior (neurotransmitters, brain regions, hormones)

In plain English: Everything you think, feel and do runs on chemical signals between brain cells, on specialized brain regions, and on hormones in the blood. Changing any of these, through damage, disease or drugs, changes behavior in predictable ways.

Analogy: The brain is a city: neurotransmitters are the text messages between buildings, brain regions are neighborhoods with jobs (the downtown office for planning, the stadium for movement), and hormones are city-wide radio broadcasts that reach everyone at once.

Official definition: Behavior depends on neurotransmitter systems, specialized and lateralized brain regions, and endocrine (hormone) systems; damage or drugs affecting these systems change mood, cognition, movement and motivation.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Neurotransmitters: dopamine (reward via VTA → nucleus accumbens; movement via substantia nigra → striatum; D₂ blockers cause parkinsonian tremor and rigidity), serotonin (mood, sleep; SSRIs), GABA (main inhibitory, the "brake"; benzodiazepines enhance it), glutamate (main excitatory, the "accelerator"; learning, LTP = long-term strengthening of synapses), acetylcholine (memory, muscle; acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which slow ACh breakdown, treat Alzheimer's), norepinephrine (arousal), endorphins (pain relief, opioid receptors).
  • Regions: frontal lobe (planning, impulse control, Broca's area; damage → impulsive, socially inappropriate), parietal (touch, spatial), temporal (hearing, Wernicke's area), occipital (vision); limbic: amygdala (fear), hippocampus (new explicit memories), hypothalamus (hunger, thirst, temperature, sex, hormones; lateral lesion → stops eating); cerebellum (balance, coordination). Left hemisphere usually dominant for language; right for spatial, face and emotional prosody (tone of voice). Split-brain: an image in the left visual field goes to the right hemisphere, so it cannot be named but can be picked out with the left hand.
  • Hormones and diseases: cortisol (adrenal cortex, stress), epinephrine (adrenal medulla), oxytocin (made in hypothalamus, released by posterior pituitary; bonding, labor, milk ejection), testosterone (dominance; rises after winning), melatonin (pineal; sleepiness in darkness). Diseases: Parkinson's (dopamine neuron loss in substantia nigra), Huntington's (CAG repeat, a stretch of DNA repeated too many times; chorea (jerky movements), mood and cognitive decline), Alzheimer's (amyloid plaques, tau tangles; education builds "cognitive reserve").

Everyday example: Scrolling a bright phone in bed at midnight tells your brain it is still daytime, so the pineal gland holds back melatonin and you lie awake. One hormone, released into the blood, changes how sleepy your whole body feels.

Worked example (step by step):

  1. A split-brain patient sees "KEY" flashed to the left visual field, so only the right hemisphere receives it.
  2. Speech is in the left hemisphere and the corpus callosum is cut, so she says "I saw nothing."
  3. Asked to reach under a screen with her left hand (controlled by the right hemisphere), she picks out the key.

MCAT trap: Mapping the visual field to the same-side hemisphere. Each visual field goes to the opposite hemisphere, and each hand is controlled by the opposite hemisphere.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (dopamine and reward), (D₂ blocker and nigrostriatal pathway), (benzodiazepines and GABA), (hippocampus), (frontal lobe injury), (lateral hypothalamus lesion), (split brain), (oxytocin), (melatonin), (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor), (Huntington's), (Parkinson's), (Alzheimer's), (glutamate).

Concept 2: Genes, environment and behavior

In plain English: Both genes and experience shape behavior, and they work together rather than separately. Twin and adoption studies let researchers estimate how much of the differences between people in a group track genetic differences, but never how much of one person's trait is "genetic".

Analogy: Genes are the seeds and environment is the soil and weather. Asking "how much of a plant's height is seed vs. soil?" has no answer for one plant, but across a field you can ask how much of the differences in height track seed differences.

Official definition: Behavior genetics uses twin, family and adoption studies to estimate heritability, the proportion of phenotypic (observed-trait) variance in a population attributable to genetic variance; genes and environments interact (diathesis–stress, gene–environment correlation) and environments can alter gene expression epigenetically.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Evidence for heritability: MZ twins reared apart are very similar; adopted children resemble biological more than adoptive parents. Twin studies may overestimate heritability because MZ twins are often treated more alike than DZ twins (violating the equal-environments assumption).
  • Genes and environment work together: gene–environment interaction: a gene variant linked to aggression (e.g. low-activity MAOA) raises aggression mainly in maltreated children. Gene–environment correlation: sociable children seek out social situations that build sociability further. Epigenetics: rat pups licked and groomed more show lasting methylation changes in stress-hormone receptor genes.
  • Concordance: schizophrenia concordance ≈ 40–50% in MZ vs. ≈ 10–15% in DZ twins: a substantial genetic contribution, but since MZ concordance is far below 100%, environment also matters.
h² ≈ 2(rMZ − rDZ)c² ≈ rMZ − h²e² ≈ 1 − rMZ

In plain words: the extra similarity of identical over fraternal twins, doubled, estimates the genetic share; whatever similarity identical twins have beyond that is the shared-home share; and whatever makes identical twins different is the unique-experience share. The three shares add up to 1.

When to use it: twin-study questions that give MZ and DZ correlations for twins raised together and ask for heritability, shared environment or non-shared environment (the "ACE" split). When it does not apply: to one individual; to twins reared apart (different formulas); when MZ twins are treated more alike than DZ twins (the estimate is then inflated). Results hold only for the population and environment studied.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
h²Heritability: share of trait variance linked to genetic variance0–1How much of the differences in the group track gene differences
c²Shared-environment share (family, home)0–1What makes siblings alike beyond genes
e²Non-shared environment share (plus measurement error)0–1What makes even identical twins differ
rMZ, rDZTrait correlations for identical and fraternal twins reared together−1 to 1MZ share ~2× the segregating (variable) genes of DZ

Everyday example: Love of spicy food. Suppose identical twins' spice ratings correlate 0.60 and fraternal twins' 0.40. h² ≈ 2(0.60 − 0.40) = 0.40; c² ≈ 0.60 − 0.40 = 0.20 (the family cooking); e² ≈ 1 − 0.60 = 0.40 (friends, travel, a bad chili night). 0.40 + 0.20 + 0.40 = 1.

MCAT worked example (step by step):

  1. For a personality trait, rMZ = 0.50 and rDZ = 0.25.
  2. h² ≈ 2(0.50 − 0.25) = 0.50; c² ≈ 0.50 − 0.50 = 0; e² ≈ 1 − 0.50 = 0.50.
  3. Check: 0.50 + 0 + 0.50 = 1. Typical for personality: about half genetic, almost no shared-family effect, the rest unique experience.

MCAT trap: "A heritability of 0.6 means 60% of a person's trait comes from genes." Heritability describes variation in a population in a particular environment, never an individual, and it can change if the environment changes.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (evidence for high heritability), (interpreting heritability 0.6), (adoption study), (twin studies overestimate), (gene–environment interaction), (gene–environment correlation), (epigenetics in rat pups), (nature vs. nurture), (schizophrenia concordance).

Concept 3: Psychoanalytic and humanistic theories of personality

In plain English: Freud said personality comes from hidden conflicts between our urges, our sense of reality and our conscience, and that we protect ourselves with unconscious tricks called defense mechanisms. Humanistic psychologists instead said people naturally grow toward their best selves when given acceptance.

Analogy: Freud's mind is a car with a wild horse (id) pulling, a strict parent in the back seat (superego) shouting rules, and a driver (ego) trying to get somewhere without crashing. Humanists say the car simply wants to reach its best destination if the road is open (self-actualization).

Official definition: Psychoanalytic theory explains personality through unconscious conflict among id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle) and superego (moral conscience), managed by defense mechanisms; humanistic theories (Rogers, Maslow) emphasize free will, growth and self-actualization.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Freud's structure and defenses: id = pleasure principle; ego = reality principle; superego = guilt and ideals (guilt at merely thinking of cheating). Defense mechanisms: repression (push thoughts out of awareness), denial (refuse to accept reality, e.g. a terminal diagnosis), projection (attribute your impulse to others), reaction formation (act opposite to the impulse: lavish sweetness to a resented mother-in-law), sublimation (channel impulses into acceptable outlets: boxing), displacement, rationalization, regression.
  • Neo-Freudians: Jung (collective unconscious, archetypes = universal symbols), Adler (inferiority complex, striving for superiority), Horney (basic anxiety, social and cultural factors), Erikson (psychosocial stages; adolescence = identity vs. role confusion). Psychoanalytic concepts are hard to test scientifically.
  • Humanistic: Rogers — anxiety arises from incongruence between the real self and the ideal self; unconditional positive regard (acceptance no matter what) helps. Maslow — self-actualization at the top of the hierarchy of needs.

Everyday example: After being dumped, a friend says "I never really liked him anyway" (rationalization), then throws herself into training for a marathon (sublimation). Both protect her from the hurt without her planning it.

Worked example (step by step):

  1. A man strongly attracted to a married coworker keeps accusing her of flirting with him.
  2. His own unacceptable impulse is attributed to her: projection.
  3. If instead he became noticeably cold and rude to her, that would be reaction formation.

MCAT trap: Mixing sublimation and displacement. Sublimation turns an impulse into a socially valued activity (boxing, surgery); displacement redirects it onto a safer target (yelling at the dog after a bad day at work).

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (id and pleasure principle), (superego guilt), (projection), (sublimation), (reaction formation), (Erikson adolescence), (Jung), (Adler), (Rogers incongruence), (unconditional positive regard), (hard to test), (self-actualization), (repression), (denial).

Concept 4: Trait, social-cognitive, behaviorist and biological theories of personality

In plain English: Some theories describe personality as a set of measurable traits; others say behavior comes from the mix of your beliefs, your past rewards and the situation; still others point to inborn temperament. The MCAT asks you to match a description to the right theory.

Analogy: Trait theory describes a person like a mixing board with five sliders (OCEAN). Social-cognitive theory adds that the music also depends on the room you play in and what you believe you can play.

Official definition: Trait theories describe personality as stable dimensions (Big Five; Eysenck's three; Allport's cardinal, central and secondary traits); social-cognitive theories explain behavior through the interaction of person, behavior and environment (reciprocal determinism), self-efficacy and locus of control; behaviorists attribute personality to reinforcement history; biological views stress temperament and arousal.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Traits: Big Five (OCEAN): openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism (anxious, moody). Eysenck: extraversion–introversion, neuroticism–stability, psychoticism. Allport: a cardinal trait dominates nearly all behavior. Mischel's critique: behavior varies across situations (person–situation debate).
  • Social-cognitive and behaviorist: Bandura: reciprocal determinism (behavior, personal factors and environment influence one another); self-efficacy ("I can master organic chemistry if I study") predicts persistence. Rotter: locus of control (internal vs. external). Behaviorists (Skinner): an outgoing child was reinforced (rewarded) for social behavior.
  • Biological and assessment: temperament (Kagan's inhibited infants become shy adults); Eysenck's arousal theory says introverts have higher baseline cortical arousal, so they avoid extra stimulation (loud parties). Assessment: objective inventories (MMPI, NEO questionnaires) vs. projective tests (TAT stories about ambiguous pictures; Rorschach inkblots).

Everyday example: Your friend is talkative at every party, every class and every family dinner: that is a stable trait (high extraversion). But she goes quiet at her strict boss's meetings: the situation matters too (Mischel's point).

Worked example (step by step):

  1. A student says "my grade depends on luck and the teacher's mood": external locus of control.
  2. A tutor helps her succeed on three quizzes in a row, and she starts saying "if I prepare, I can do this": rising self-efficacy.
  3. She studies longer, which raises grades further: person, behavior and environment feeding each other (reciprocal determinism).

MCAT trap: Confusing self-efficacy (belief about ability on a specific task) with self-esteem (overall self-worth) or with locus of control (belief about what causes outcomes).

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (Big Five), (neuroticism), (cardinal trait), (situational critique), (Eysenck), (introvert arousal), (reciprocal determinism), (self-efficacy), (behaviorist view), (temperament), (projective test), (external locus of control).

Concept 5: Models of disorder, schizophrenia and mood disorders

In plain English: Psychological disorders are diagnosed from lists of symptoms and how long they last. Most arise from a mix of biology, thinking patterns and life stress. Schizophrenia involves losing touch with reality; mood disorders involve long stretches of depression or abnormally high mood.

Analogy: The diathesis–stress model is a glass already partly full (vulnerability); stressors pour in more water. A disorder appears when the glass overflows, so a fuller glass needs less stress to spill.

Official definition: Psychological disorders are classified in the DSM-5 by symptom criteria and duration; the biomedical model emphasizes physical causes and treatments, the biopsychosocial model combines biological, psychological and social factors, and the diathesis–stress model proposes that disorders arise when vulnerability meets stress.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Schizophrenia: positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions such as ideas of reference — the news anchor sends personal messages — disorganized speech) vs. negative symptoms (flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia). Duration ≥ 6 months with ≥ 1 month active symptoms; brief psychotic disorder lasts < 1 month. Dopamine hypothesis (D₂ blockers reduce positive symptoms; amphetamines worsen them); enlarged ventricles (fluid spaces in the brain); MZ concordance ≈ 40–50%.
  • Depression: major depressive disorder ≥ 2 weeks (depressed mood or anhedonia + other symptoms); persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) ≥ 2 years of milder symptoms; seasonal pattern (winter). Theories: monoamine (serotonin, norepinephrine; SSRIs), Seligman's learned helplessness, Beck's cognitive triad (negative views of self, world, future).
  • Bipolar: bipolar I requires at least one manic episode (≥ 1 week, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, risky spending); bipolar II requires hypomania (≥ 4 days) plus major depression. Lithium is the classic mood stabilizer.

Everyday example: Everyone has a sad week after a breakup; that is not a disorder. If the low mood, loss of interest and poor sleep last every day for over 2 weeks and stop you working, it meets the time and impairment test for major depression. Duration is the dividing line.

Worked example (step by step, DSM durations):

  1. A man has had a decreased need for sleep (2 h/night), rapid speech and reckless spending for 8 days.
  2. 8 days ≥ 7 days → a full manic episode → bipolar I.
  3. If the same symptoms had lasted 4 days without marked impairment, it would be hypomania (≥ 4 days), fitting bipolar II if major depression had also occurred.

MCAT trap: Calling flat affect a positive symptom because it is "obvious." Positive means added experiences (hallucinations, delusions); negative means missing normal functions (flat affect, alogia, avolition).

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (biomedical approach), (biopsychosocial), (diathesis–stress), (DSM-5 basis), (positive symptom), (negative symptoms), (delusion of reference), (dopamine hypothesis), (enlarged ventricles), (brief psychotic disorder), (MDD duration), (persistent depressive disorder), (bipolar I vs. II), (manic episode), (lithium), (Beck).

Concept 6: Anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, trauma, dissociative, somatic, personality and neurocognitive disorders

In plain English: Beyond schizophrenia and mood disorders, the DSM groups disorders by their main feature: too much fear, repeated unwanted thoughts and rituals, reactions to trauma, breaks in memory or identity, physical symptoms driven by worry, long-standing rigid personality patterns, and declines in thinking. The timing rules separate many of them.

Analogy: Anxiety disorders are an overeager smoke alarm: it rings when there is no fire, and running away (avoidance) "proves" the alarm right because nothing bad happens, so it keeps ringing next time.

Official definition: Anxiety disorders involve excessive fear or worry (generalized anxiety, panic disorder, agoraphobia, specific phobias); OCD and related disorders, trauma- and stressor-related disorders, dissociative, somatic symptom, personality (clusters A, B, C) and neurocognitive disorders (delirium, dementia) are separate DSM-5 categories.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Anxiety and OCD: GAD: excessive worry about many things for ≥ 6 months. Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks plus worry about more; agoraphobia: avoiding places where escape is hard. Phobias are acquired by classical conditioning (dog bite) and maintained by avoidance (negative reinforcement: escaping the fear rewards avoiding). OCD (obsessions + compulsions, e.g. checking the stove) is grouped with body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding and trichotillomania (hair pulling), not with anxiety disorders.
  • Trauma, dissociative, somatic: PTSD: intrusions (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, negative mood and cognition, hyperarousal, lasting > 1 month (3 days to 1 month = acute stress disorder). Dissociative: amnesia with fugue (new identity elsewhere), depersonalization/derealization (feeling unreal or detached), dissociative identity disorder. Somatic: conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom: sudden arm paralysis with normal tests), illness anxiety disorder (few symptoms, fear of disease), somatic symptom disorder (real symptoms + excessive worry).
  • Personality and neurocognitive: Cluster A odd (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), B dramatic (antisocial — pattern since age 15, adult diagnosis, no remorse; borderline — unstable relationships, abandonment fear, self-harm, splitting (all-good or all-bad views); histrionic; narcissistic — craves admiration, no empathy), C anxious (avoidant — wants friends but fears rejection; dependent; OCPD — perfectionism, ego-syntonic). Ego-syntonic traits cause little distress. Neurocognitive: delirium (acute, fluctuating attention, often reversible) vs. dementia (gradual, progressive).

Everyday example: A child bitten by a dog starts crossing the street whenever she sees one. Each time she crosses, her fear drops, which rewards the avoidance, so she never learns most dogs are friendly. That is how a phobia is learned (conditioning) and kept (avoidance).

Worked example (step by step, PTSD timing):

  1. A soldier has flashbacks, nightmares and hypervigilance starting after combat.
  2. At 2 weeks (between 3 days and 1 month), the diagnosis is acute stress disorder.
  3. If the same symptoms are still present at 6 weeks (> 1 month), the diagnosis becomes PTSD.

MCAT trap: Delirium vs. dementia. Delirium is acute and fluctuating, with impaired attention, often from medication or infection, and is often reversible. Dementia is gradual and progressive.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (GAD), (agoraphobia), (phobia by conditioning), (avoidance maintains phobia), (OCD), (OCD grouping), (body dysmorphic disorder), (PTSD clusters), (acute stress disorder), (dissociative fugue), (conversion disorder), (illness anxiety), (three clusters), (borderline), (antisocial), (avoidant), (OCPD vs. OCD), (dementia), (delirium), (panic disorder).

Concept 7: Theories of motivation and hunger

In plain English: Different theories explain why we act: to satisfy body needs, to keep excitement at a comfortable level, to earn outside rewards, or to grow as a person. Hunger is a good test case, run by two hypothalamus areas and two hormones.

Analogy: Drives push you from behind (hunger pushes you to the kitchen); incentives pull you from in front (the smell of pizza draws you in even when full); arousal theory says you are always adjusting a thermostat for excitement.

Official definition: Motivation is explained by instinct theory (innate patterns), drive-reduction theory (reducing tension from unmet biological needs to restore homeostasis), arousal theory (seeking an optimal arousal level), incentive theory (external rewards pull behavior), Maslow's hierarchy and self-determination theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness).

Core idea (3 points):

  • Classic theories: instinct theory was criticized for naming behaviors rather than explaining them. Drive reduction cannot explain thrill-seeking or curiosity (which raise tension); arousal theory and Yerkes–Dodson can (optimal arousal; complex tasks need lower arousal). Incentive theory: a $10,000 scholarship motivates more than a $500 one.
  • Needs and intrinsic motivation: Maslow: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem (respect, competence) → self-actualization; lower needs generally come first (a man who lost his home focuses on safety). Self-determination theory: intrinsic motivation needs autonomy, competence and relatedness. Overjustification effect: rewarding an already enjoyable activity lowers intrinsic motivation. Need for achievement: preference for moderate difficulty and feedback.
  • Hunger and other drives: lateral hypothalamus starts eating (lesion → stop eating); ventromedial hypothalamus stops eating (lesion → overeating). Ghrelin (empty stomach) raises hunger; leptin (from fat cells) signals satiety (fullness). Opponent-process theory explains drug tolerance and withdrawal (the opposing after-reaction grows with use). Conflicts: approach–avoidance (far-away prestigious college), avoidance–avoidance (two disliked chores).

Everyday example: You just finished a big dinner and feel full (leptin and a full stomach), yet you still order dessert when the waiter brings the cake tray. Drive reduction says you should stop; incentive theory explains the "dessert stomach".

Worked example (step by step, overjustification):

  1. Children who already love drawing draw 6 pictures a day.
  2. They are paid $1 per picture for a week; after payment ends they draw 3 a day.
  3. Drop = (6 − 3)/6 = 50%. The reward shifted the reason for drawing from "fun" to "money," so intrinsic motivation fell: overjustification.

MCAT trap: Using drive-reduction theory to explain skydiving or curiosity. Those behaviors increase arousal; arousal theory, not drive reduction, explains them.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (drive reduction), (hard for drive reduction), (incentive theory), (instinct theory critique), (Yerkes–Dodson), (Maslow base), (esteem needs), (self-determination theory), (overjustification), (need for achievement), (leptin), (ghrelin), (opponent-process), (approach–avoidance), (arousal theory).

Concept 8: Attitudes and behavior

In plain English: An attitude is how you feel about, act toward and think about something. Attitudes often fail to predict what people actually do, and, surprisingly, what we do often changes our attitudes, especially when we cannot explain our behavior any other way.

Analogy: An attitude is a three-legged stool: how you feel (affect), what you do (behavior), and what you believe (cognition). If one leg gets out of line with the others (dissonance), you shift a leg to stop wobbling.

Official definition: Attitudes have affective, behavioral and cognitive components (ABC model). Attitudes predict behavior best when strong, specific, accessible (easily brought to mind) and formed by experience; behavior also shapes attitudes through cognitive dissonance, self-perception, role-playing and the foot-in-the-door effect.

Core idea (3 points):

  • ABC and the attitude–behavior gap: affect ("I love recycling"), behavior ("I recycle"), cognition ("I believe recycling reduces landfill waste"). LaPiere's study: businesses served a Chinese couple in person but said in letters they would refuse, an early demonstration of the attitude–behavior gap. Implicit attitudes (IAT, the Implicit Association Test, which uses response times) can differ from reported ones. Theory of planned behavior: attitude + subjective norms + perceived behavioral control → intention → behavior.
  • Behavior → attitude: Festinger and Carlsmith's $1 vs. $20 study (low pay = insufficient justification = more attitude change), post-decision dissonance (rating the chosen job higher after choosing), smokers adding new cognitions ("it helps me control my weight"), role-playing (arguing an assigned side), foot-in-the-door (a small request first makes a big one more likely). Self-perception theory (Bem): we infer our attitudes from watching our own behavior.
  • Persuasion: elaboration likelihood model: central route (argument quality, high motivation and ability) gives durable change; peripheral route (attractiveness, credentials) gives weaker, short-lived change. Situational pressures (neighbor's lawn) can override strong attitudes.

Everyday example: You pay $300 for concert tickets, then the show is mediocre. Instead of admitting you wasted the money, you tell everyone "it was actually amazing". Spending so much with no good result creates dissonance, so your attitude shifts to match what you did.

Worked example (step by step):

  1. Participants do a boring task and are paid $1 or $20 to tell the next person it was fun (Festinger and Carlsmith, 1959).
  2. Later, on a scale from −5 (boring) to +5 (enjoyable), the $1 group rated it +1.35, the $20 group −0.05, and unpaid controls −0.45.
  3. The $1 group had no good external reason for lying, so they reduced dissonance by changing their attitude.

MCAT trap: Predicting that the larger payment produces more attitude change. With a big reward the lie is justified; dissonance, and therefore attitude change, is greatest with insufficient justification.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (ABC model), (cognitive component), ($1 vs. $20), (when attitudes predict behavior), (foot-in-the-door), (role-playing), (theory of planned behavior), (smoker adds cognitions), (self-perception), (peripheral route), (implicit attitudes), (LaPiere), (post-decision dissonance).

C) 3 MCAT-STYLE PRACTICE QUESTIONS

Q1. A researcher pays children to draw with markers, an activity they already enjoyed. When payment stops, they draw less than before. Which concept explains this?

  • A) Drive-reduction theory
  • B) Overjustification effect
  • C) Cognitive dissonance
  • D) Learned helplessness

Answer: B. An external reward undermined intrinsic motivation.

  • A is wrong: drawing does not reduce a biological drive.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: dissonance would increase liking for a behavior done with insufficient reward.
  • D is wrong: learned helplessness follows uncontrollable negative events.

Q2. A patient hears voices commenting on her actions and believes neighbors are broadcasting her thoughts. She also has flat affect and little speech. Which symptom list is correct?

  • A) Positive: flat affect; negative: hallucinations
  • B) Positive: hallucinations and delusions; negative: flat affect and alogia
  • C) All four are negative symptoms
  • D) All four are positive symptoms

Answer: B. Positive symptoms add experiences (hallucinations, delusions); negative symptoms are deficits (flat affect, alogia, avolition).

  • A is wrong: it swaps the categories.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: hallucinations and delusions are positive.
  • D is wrong: flat affect and alogia are negative.

Q3. A student believes her exam grade depends mostly on luck and on the teacher's mood. Which concept describes this belief, and in which theory is it rooted?

  • A) External locus of control; Rotter's social learning theory
  • B) Low self-esteem; humanistic theory
  • C) Neuroticism; trait theory
  • D) Reaction formation; psychoanalytic theory

Answer: A. Attributing outcomes to outside forces is an external locus of control (Rotter).

  • A is correct.
  • B is wrong: self-esteem is self-evaluation, not beliefs about causes of outcomes.
  • C is wrong: neuroticism is emotional instability, a trait, not a causal belief.
  • D is wrong: reaction formation is acting opposite to an unacceptable impulse.
